claims.text: The anomalous strain-rate insensitivity of yield strength is driven by thermally activated collective glide of super-dislocations through a heterogeneous CSRO landscape.
FCC-to-BCC phase transformation is not the primary mechanism controlling yield onset.
Simple dislocation nucleation is not the primary mechanism controlling yield onset.
Yield stress is governed by the energy barrier for cutting through local CSRO clusters.
Collective dislocation motion has a high activation volume that produces weak strain-rate dependence.
The initial alloy is a fully annealed single-crystal FCC phase.
The initial alloy contains significant CSRO.
The initial alloy contains no pre-existing BCC phase and no significant dislocation density.
CSRO clusters act as strong, thermally activated pinning points for dislocation motion.
Dislocations must cut through or bypass CSRO clusters to glide.
Thermal activation over the CSRO-related barrier, rather than phonon or electron drag, is the rate-limiting process.
Yield strength decreases strongly as temperature increases from 77 K toward 600 K.
Yield strength changes negligibly over strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^2 s^-1.
No BCC diffraction peaks emerge during the elastic-to-plastic transition.
FCC diffraction peaks broaden during yielding because of lattice distortion and dislocation accumulation.
Pure Ni and Cu exhibit a moderate positive yield-strength correlation with strain rate due to phonon drag and weaker temperature dependence than the HEA.
Second-phase precipitates or entry into an athermal high-rate regime may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Potential orientation anisotropy is to be evaluated for loading along [100], [110], and [111], but no orientation-specific validity constraint is stated.
Observation of distinct BCC peaks at yield onset would falsify the claim that CSRO-controlled dislocation glide, rather than transformation, is the primary deformation mode.
A coherent BCC phase fraction greater than 1% in the plastic zone is treated as evidence that phase transformation is the primary deformation mode.
